headline: Biddeford Pool Incoming Hour Still Owns July — Bass to 28, Blues Crash Higgins on Bunker
subhead: A neap tide softened the rips but the bass never got the memo — and the bluefish finally found the beach in daylight.
body_markdown:
Tuesday evening, incoming tide at the Pool, a guy I've fished next to for maybe fifteen years hooks a bass on a black-and-purple Danny plug that damn near pulled him off the rock. Twenty-eight inches, fat as a football, came up through that channel current like it owned the place. That's the Pool doing what the Pool does on the last two hours of the flood — bait gets squeezed through the gut between the beach and the ledges, and the bass sit right on that seam waiting for the buffet line to start. Best hour of the striper day in this state, and it hasn't slowed down one bit.

We're coming off the first-quarter neap now, which means the big swings are behind us for the moment and the current through spots like the Pool channel and the Saco River mouth isn't ripping the way it was two weeks back. That's not a bad thing. Softer current widens the window — instead of a tight forty-five minutes where the plug bite turns on, I'm getting closer to ninety minutes of good water on both sides of peak flood. If you've been showing up right at the tide change and leaving disappointed, push your window out. The fish are more forgiving right now, not less.

Cooler Gulf of Maine water is still the story north of Boston, and it's the reason this whole stretch is fishing better in daylight than anything south of the Cape right now. Down in the warmer water they're pushing bass into night-only patterns. Up here the fish are still willing to eat at ten in the morning if the bait's moving. I had a solid daytime session off Prouts Neck this week on a southwest wind — that wind pushes a little chop onto the outside rocks and gets the bass feeding up on top, chasing pogies right in the wash. Threw a Gibbs Pencil Popper, walked it through the froth off the eastern side near the point, and connected on three fish in the 24 to 26-inch range before the wind swung and killed it. Southwest breeze under 15 knots is the number to watch for that spot — any harder and it gets unfishable off those rocks.

The blues showed up at Higgins Beach this week, and this is exactly the pattern we said was coming — bunker schools working up the coast, blues riding right behind them, and once that bait pushes into range of a beach the blitz follows. Wednesday morning, bunch of guys standing in the wash at Higgins watching pogies get shredded thirty yards off the sand. Blues in the 3 to 6-pound class, gorging hard enough that you could throw damn near anything and get bit. I did best on a 1-ounce Deadly Dick worked fast just under the surface — the erratic wobble matches a wounded pogy better than most swimmers. If you're chasing that blitz, watch the water off Higgins and Pine Point in the early morning — bunker pods show as dark nervous patches, and the birds working over them will tell you before your eyes do.

Mackerel are still thick off Wells Harbor and Ogunquit, schooling tight around the harbor mouths and out past the breakwaters. That bait is doing double duty — it's keeping the striper feed going even where bunker haven't pushed in yet, and it's good enough eating that a lot of guys are jigging strictly for macks with small diamond jigs or Sabiki rigs off the rocks. If you want a bass instead, tip a bucktail with a mackerel strip and work it along the current edges outside Wells Harbor on the last of the outgoing — that combination has been quietly productive while everybody's chasing the blitz noise.

Down on the flats, Pine Point mud has been giving up decent flounder on sandworms and clam bellies fished on a simple two-hook flounder rig, best on the slower water either side of dead low. Nothing spectacular in size, but steady enough for a bucket if you're patient and willing to move around the flat looking for the softer mud pockets where they hold.

Cod fishing stays a boat game right now — the ledges off Cape Elizabeth are producing for guys jigging deep with diamond jigs or dropping bait rigs down 80 to 120 feet, but it's not a beach story and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Looking ahead, if this southwest wind pattern holds through the weekend, I'd be at Prouts Neck early with topwater plugs before the breeze builds past that 15-knot mark. And I'd still make the Pool incoming my anchor session — with the neap softening the current, that window's forgiving enough to fish twice a day if you've got the legs for it. The bunker are still pushing north, so don't be surprised if Pine Point and the stretch toward Kennebunk start showing the same blitz behavior Higgins had this week. Bring the Danny plugs, bring the Pencil Poppers, and watch the birds.
